title: Full agentic game development. I don’t think we are there yet
author: ggrmx
selftext:
I have been running an experiment with a side project of mine.

I set up a software factory to see how it handles building a game from scratch, while trying to make something beyond a tech demo and have an acceptable quality.

I’ve been running the factory almost 24/7 for 3 weeks and only stops when i hit the usage limit from claude.

The GDD was defined by me and claude wrote the specs (which i reviewed).

The game is like an strategy game (think something like civilization), no physics or crazy character movement, that I assume agents can handle well.

Using claude and codex.

Setup is :

Queue of tasks based on milestones 

spec agent prepare the task -> implementer agent -> 2 agent reviewers (ui and logic) then merge.

I have milestones goals where I manually test and raise new issues.

I encounter a few problems, like the implementer not following skills that are defined or faking tests (it hid an  screenshots from the reviewer agent for example) and hallucinations (references to skills that do not exist and stuff like that).

But my main concern is how exponential in time and consumption (tokens) each change or improvement takes when the project increases in complexity. I think  it will get unmanageable and some point.

I don’t take this a total failure. The game works good enough to test the play loop and ideas, and I believe for simpler games same setup can provide excellent results.

I’ll see how the following days go, if this as a dead end I will salvage what I can and restart the project with better foundations and using ai as a assist rather than letting it rip by itself.

Let me know if you have done something similar as this, it might had worked better for you.

Cheers

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
I think this is pretty well-known. Having somebody write a GDD and then hand it off to an AI? Yeah, it doesn’t work. You could try making the GDD more detailed but that is kind of a rookie mistake.

> But my main concern is how exponential in time and consumption (tokens) each change or improvement takes when the project increases in complexity. I think it will get unmanageable and some point. 

This is avoidable. You’re just getting that because your software factory isn’t dealing with maintainability issues. This isn’t a completely solved problem but I am going to guess that there are a lot of problems here that are caused by deficiencies in your software factory—missing workflows, perhaps.

**edit** I’ll add that the experiment of vibe-coding a game with just a GDD is educational even if it is obvious that it will fail.

replies.author: ggrmx
replies.body:
Thanks for the input 

I provided more than the original gdd, that was only to kickstart the project definition. I continued having conversations with it until I have a clear milestone 0 of what I want.

The milestone 0 was accomplished without major issues, but when I started adding after that it started getting worse over time.

The ai still hallucinates and produce stuff that wasn’t defined anywhere or even ignore skills.

I made it take small retros after specific numbers of tasks completed to improve and fix issues in the software factory.

I’m still testing it to see if this approach is usuable for me

replies.author: 3tt07kjt
replies.body:
“More than the GDD” is exactly the rookie mistake I mentioned. It was the wrong way to make games before AI, and it’s still wrong now that we have AI.

Problems with hallucinations are often tied to problems like too much context. 

The AI should be building stuff that isn’t defined anywhere. That’s useful. Otherwise you would have to define everything.

comments.author: Lavio00
comments.body:
AI is unimaginably bad at judgement. It is really, really good at implementation, but only insofar as it is clear what you want to implement. 

The *road* to implementation does not have to be known by you—AI is fairly good at planning that itself—but the goal needs be be clearly defined or it totally shits the bed. This goes for Fable 5.2, too.

So, of course fully agentic wont work, because that implies it would have the capacity to judge if what it produced is what you want. The less generic you want something to be, the more involved you have to be.

comments.author: hydroxyHU
comments.body: I feel the same way. Two months ago, I started developing a historical castle defense game; I wanted to base it on the tough decisions in Frostpunk, with my own economic mechanics and etching-style graphics. At first, everything was going great, but as the complexity grew, the whole thing started to fall apart from one playtest to the next. We rewrote several subsystems multiple times—sometimes pushing them to the background, other times making them more prominent—but the whole thing just wouldn’t come together. On top of that, Claude likes to slack off sometimes, and it doesn’t always implement everything; just one or two things get left out. Then, when we build on those, the documentation, the game in my head, and the implemented feature start living three completely different lives. So, after two months of trying, I set the game aside, and now I’ve been working on a smaller-scale mangaka career simulator for nearly 10 days—so far, this is the closest I’ve come to a playable demo. But this requires incredibly strict scope management and multiple rounds of quality checks.

comments.author: VictorBuildsApps
comments.body:
The hiding-evidence problem is the one I would fix first: don't let the implementer produce what the reviewer looks at. On my current jam game the reviewer runs its own probe against a snapshot of the code in headless Chromium and counts overlapping HUD elements frame by frame, on the old build and the new one with the same seed.

Today that caught a fix that cleared the problem it was written for and made another one worse. Captions moved off a countdown plate, but at 1024x640 with 150% text they ran into the card chips: 407 overlapping frame pairs before, 696 after.

It doesn't fix your cost growth. The point is that the reviewer sees measurements it took itself, not what the implementer chose to show.

comments.author: DaedalusRaistlin
comments.body:
I've made over 30 game prototypes in the last 5 months or so with Claude. In my experience the GDD gets you the prototype and that's it. 

I'm actively working on about 4 of those games, because it really needs a different approach. You need to sit down and thoroughly review everything that works and what doesn't. Then you need to plan out a roadmap of features you want to implement. Organise them by milestones and choose which are the most important. 

The AI can't really test the feel, and it usually just takes screenshots so it misses movement of objects and other related issues. It can't test if the core gameplay is fun. 

If you try to ask it to make a fun game, in my experience it makes something boring. I once asked Gemini to make a game that was fun and exciting using recent trends and it gave me a 2048 style numbers game. Apparently that's what it considered exciting.

After the prototype comes heavy iteration, and I feel the AI models just aren't good at recognising visual and gameplay issues. I often have to pause the game and go "look at the scene and tell me why (this unrealistic thing is happening)", because it never occurred to the AI that it would look silly, like walls and objects floating in mid-air after building destruction. A rather silly one was textures being world mapped for debris pieces so they looked wierd, like a reflection moving smoothly across the surface.

comments.author: Arcodiant
comments.body: The pain point I'm hitting is around testing; I've built lots of playtest tools for the agents to iterate on the game as it's working, but it tends to fixate on pixel-matching scenes and adding ever more tests to every pass, and the whole thing gets bogged down. I working on getting the agents to be more focused and efficient, but it's slow going.

comments.author: sunnystormy64
comments.body: You're doing it wrong. You sound like you just want to push a button and have AI automate everything without any additional thought / effort from you, and that tells me that you don't understand AI at all. Collaboration with AI is a combination of dialogue and pedagogy. It's like playing tennis: you NEED a back-and-forth rhythm to make things enjoyable, and the higher the velocity, the more fun / challenging it becomes. Hearing you setting yourself up for failure and then coming onto this sub to complain that "we aren't there yet" (your post's title), when there are plenty of us (myself included) making magic with AI, reeks of low effort and skill issues.

replies.author: ggrmx
replies.body:
Did I complain anywhere?

Even the title have the part “I think” not a statement. Marked the post as discussion and looked for how other people are experiencing with it.

Why did you assume I didn’t have a back and forth with the ai?

comments.author: TheVoyant
comments.body:
Build the tools and structure to make the game first. You have to take the decision making out of their hands and steer them.

If you let Ai Invent you will always end up with a circus of problems, because it cannot keep scope or full vision of the project. 

You have to manage them, even if left to automate. 

Once you have a full devkit built for your game you can trust agents to do what you need with simple instructions. Because you're not letting it invent, its working within your system.

replies.author: ggrmx
replies.body: Yes, i think that setting up the tools and systems first will be the way to go for me

comments.author: shimroot
comments.body:
A game isn’t a SaaS that solves a problem. AI is amazing at building the tech part of the game. The fun part is on you. 

If you don’t playtest it continously to ensure it’s enjoyable and you’re actually having fun with it, the AI will produce a great tech product that’s boring as hell and no one cares about.

replies.author: ggrmx
replies.body: I do play test it all the time though, but each change keeps on increasing in time and complexity.

replies.author: shimroot
replies.body:
And do you ask the model to do changes based on how the game feels? Most of the time I spend working with AI is to nitpick on things that don’t feel good, not on big items. And when this becomes too tedious or recurring I ask it to build me a tool to do it manually, not spend endless tokens going back and forth.

i.e. for my racing game I have a config where I can manually tweak car and surface settings so I can quickly test things without needing anything else

replies.author: ggrmx
replies.body: I like the idea of the tools to do it manually. I don’t know why i didn’t think about it, as I have done similar things in the past. Thanks

replies.author: shimroot
replies.body:
And maybe another thing that might be of help: tests. Add/change test after you’re happy with how something works. And add mutation tests to test the tests. 

Having a big suite of tests that the agent can run helps a lot with debugging and token consumption.

comments.author: Ok_Feedback4200
comments.body: Sorry but I read this as user error. Claude is already there.

comments.author: ChadSexman
comments.body:
I’ve shifted my technique to waterfall style and I’m having much better results.

Design > adversarial review x3 > technical spec > adversarial review x2 > epic/task sequencing > build

Then let it cook for a few days.

The more detail in your GDD, the better results. Also invest early in your CICD and review pipeline.

As an added note; build yourself a token tracking system, so you can see precisely what you are burning tokens on. Fable is pretty good at suggesting improvements. After a few rounds, it cut my daily spend by about half.

comments.author: TheLastNeonDev
comments.body: same feeling here tbh. 5 months in and build 170, and most of the real fixes came from playtests not specs. stuff like the game feeling empty between jobs, no agent was gonna notice that on its own

comments.author: Mrbuttshaman
comments.body: For me it helped to have a few things.  First I came up with a game plan for what I wanted, then made a game design document.  Then I refined that until it matched pretty much exactly what I wanted.  Then I have a 6 hour interrogation on every element of that, from UI, interface, perspective, resolution preferences, storytelling tone,  story telling conventions, style and style cohesion, etc.  I feed it documents that I've had other session prepare that I have them reference.  Things about core systems, my preferred writing style, my asset generation pipelines, my agent preferences, etc. After all of the interrogation, and if there are no additional questions, then I basically make a low level demo of the most core gameplay loop and make it build it out. That's with nothing, no art, nothing, its all place holder and its ugly and doesn't have sound effects.  I tweak that until I can play it over and over and actually have fun with it.  After that, I expand it with a ton of different ideas to add variety and make sure each of those things are fun in isolation with nothing else to distract me.  All of this is super lightweight and uses almost nothing in tokens.  I can get by with sonnet 95% of the time with this iteration loop.  Most of my time is me playtesting and making it fun.  Then I have it make a sample narrative scene in engine(I'm making some narrative stuff and fed it google research papers on theater), if that passes my vetting process, I basically make sure it can produce assets that maintain stylistic consistency using comfy\_UI and commercially viable models and have it write up the overall story and everything and let it expand wildly to build out the rest of the game largely by itself.  Basically the big hurdle is making the core game loop fun and repeatable without any of the frills and making sure you can produce an understanding with claude and concept art that allows you to create repeatable and consistent successes in content creation before you let it run wild.  You have to tweak far less later if you do that. Passing lessons from one agent to another by having them use a shared scratchpad has also been extremely helpful when I'm working on multiple projects.

replies.author: ggrmx
replies.body:
Thanks for the advice.  
I’m still refining my process, it just exponentially takes more time per task, so my progress has slowed down significantly.

I think i need to move my core gameloop out to a lighter ui to refine the gameplay, and then put the work in the u when that has been cooked. i don’t mind placeholder art during dev process

replies.author: Mrbuttshaman
replies.body: Yea I'm more just saying for me it was important to get a tight loop and gradually expand each tight loop into an outer loop with more and more interconnected systems.  It's hard to polish each component before expanding and it isn't nearly as satisfying as trying to one shot something to get something playable on a large scale but if you build out too early without getting far enough tightening it, then everything built on it gets more and more shakey and cost more and more to correct which you seem to be aware of.  Anyway, I wish you the best of luck.  It's definitely a continual learning process.
